title: The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · s0001-p1】Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) is an RNA editing enzyme that catalyzes the deamination of adenosine, converting it to inosine. This type of adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing occurs primarily within Alu-rich double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), thereby preventing aberrant activation of innate immune sensing of endogenous dsRNA. 1 , 2 Dysregulated ADAR1 editing activity has been linked to cancer cell fitness, immune evasion and therapy resistance across multiple cancer types, including breast, liver, esophageal, colorectal, lung, and head and neck cancers. 3-7 The majority of the published work emphasized ADAR1's RNA editing function as the dominant mechanism by which ADAR1 promotes tumor growth and immune escape. These aspects are well covered in recent reviews and remain fundamental. 8‐11 Yet, in more recent years, editing-independent functions mediated through other domains of ADAR1 have also moved to the foreground. Several recent reviews have begun to discuss more comprehensively, both editing-dependent and editing-independent roles of ADAR1 in cancer biology. 12 , 13

【Introduction · s0001-p2】Importantly, ADAR1 exists as two major isoforms: the constitutive, predominantly nuclear p110 isoform and the interferon (IFN)-inducible, predominantly cytoplasmic p150 isoform. Large-scale genome-wide shRNA and CRISPR/Cas9 screening datasets, such as the Project DRIVE 14 and Cancer Dependency Map, 15 as well as independent loss-of-function studies, have repeatedly identified ADAR1 as a cancer dependency enriched in IFN-high contexts. 16‐19 Through our own functional genomic work in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), we provided strong evidence that the IFN can sensitize non-dependent OSCC to the loss of ADAR1, while the expression of the ADAR1-p150 (but not p110) can potently reverse the ADAR1 knockout-induced lethality phenotype. 17 This provides a strong rationale for targeting the IFN-inducible p150 isoform as an effective and specific therapeutic approach in ADAR1-dependent cancers. 17 , 20 In support of this, isoform resolved analyses demonstrated that p150 edits a broader and distinct set of RNA substrates 21 and occupies distinct interaction networks compared with p110, 20 despite sharing an identical deaminase domain. This suggests that both isoforms impact transcription in their unique ways.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Z-nucleic acids (ZNAs) and the Zα domain in ADAR1 · s0001-s2001-p3】Structurally, ADAR1-p150's Zα adopts a winged helix–turn–helix fold which consists of three α-helices packed against a small β-sheet. This pre-formed binding surface interacts with the zig-zag backbone of ZNAs through a network of electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions (Figure 1B). 37 , 54 , 55 , 62 Within ADAR1-p150 Zα, there are several conserved residues, namely N173, Y177, P193 and W195 which are collectively central to ZNAs binding, recognition and structural integrity, which hold translational relevance. 54 , 63 Within α3 helix, N173 is key to high-affinity nucleic acid binding, as it is pre‑organized in the orientation that favor ADAR1-p150 to engage Z‑RNA efficiently. N173A mutation markedly reduces binding affinity and the N173S variant is linked to Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS). 64 On the other hand, Y177 helps distinguish between RNA and DNA and also contributes to the recognition of the Z‑form over B-form nucleic acid. 54 , 62 Within the β-sheet, P193 helps maintain the structural architecture by restricting loop flexibility and ensuring proper positioning of the recognition surface. Clinically, P193A mutation is often observed in patients with AGS and bilateral striatal necrosis. 65 W195 helps stabilise the structural scaffold of Zα and is required for effective Z-RNA recognition. W195A (W197A in mouse) mutation disrupts Z-RNA binding and causes massive degradation of the protein inside the cell which results in AGS-like inflammatory phenotypes in vivo. 66 Collectively, these key residues provide a rational structural basis for the development of Zα-targeting drugs. Although limited, early virtual screening and binding-based studies support the tractability of this domain as a pharmacological target, reinforcing its emerging relevance in isoform-selective ADAR1-p150 targeting strategies. 29‐31,67‐69

【Therapeutic targeting of ADAR1-Zα · s0002-p4】ADAR1-p150 has been identified as the dominant isoform responsible for A-to-I RNA editing, preferentially targeting 3′ UTR regions of mRNAs, due to its localization in the cytoplasm. This editing activity by ADAR1-p150 is sufficient to prevent the activation of PKR and MDA5 during IFN signaling, thereby suppressing lethal auto-immunity and maintaining cellular homeostasis. 21 , 60 , 76 , 111 , 113 Among current strategies, Rebecsinib employs the isoform-selective mechanism (Figure 2-B1). Rebecsinib is a splice-modulating agent that specifically attenuates ADAR1-p150 expression thereby limiting p150-dependent cytoplasmic RNA editing. In leukemia cells, Rebecsinib restores innate immune sensing and disrupts leukemia stem cell maintenance while preserving ADAR1-p110 activity in maintaining homeostasis. Its efficacy was subsequently tested in humanized leukemia mouse models. 115 Importantly, Rebecsinib has now progressed beyond preclinical evaluation, with a first-in-human Phase 1 trial of Rebecsinib (NCT07250646) currently recruiting patients with relapsed/refractory secondary acute myeloid leukemia or high-risk myelofibrosis. This study represents an important step towards the clinical translation of ADAR1-targeted therapies. The N-terminus of ADAR1-p150 contains a nuclear export signal that allows the protein to shuttle to the cytoplasm, where it inhibits ZBP1-mediated signalling. By preventing ADAR1-p150 from entering the cytoplasm, nuclear export inhibitors such as Selinexor (KPT-330) and Eltanexor (KPT-8602) have been shown to perturb ADAR1-p150-associated ZBP1 regulation and activate PANoptotic pathways in cell-based melanoma and immune-cell models. Their therapeutic effects were further supported in preclinical melanoma tumor models, particularly in combination with IFNs, where nuclear export inhibition increased tumor cell death and reduced tumor volume (Figure 2-B2). 71 , 116 However, because these agents broadly inhibit XPO1-mediated nuclear export, their effects are not specific to ADAR1-p150 and likely involve additional cellular pathways beyond ADAR1 regulation. Together, these approaches demonstrate that selective interference with ADAR1-p150 is feasible and therapeutically meaningful. This therefore represents a critical gap where more specific and selective inhibition of the Zα domain is warranted. Given that AGS-associated Zα mutations, like N173S and P193A (P195A in mouse), are sufficient to trigger an immune response even when the catalytic domain remains intact. 61 , 64 , 65 This genetic evidence demonstrates that ZNAs sensing is a regulatory function distinct from catalytic editing, suggesting that specifically blocking this domain could selectively activate innate immunity in tumors while preserving essential editing.

evidence.section: Z-nucleic acids (ZNAs) and the Zα domain in ADAR1

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · s0004-p1】Although many mechanistic gaps remain, developing Zα-specific inhibitors that selectively target ADAR1-p150 offers a strategy to suppress tumor growth without significantly affecting the constitutively expressed ADAR1-p110 isoform in normal cells. From a translational perspective, the ADAR1–Zα–ZNAs axis is an underexplored yet promising therapeutic pathway. However, many potential ADAR1-Zα inhibitors are still in early phase of pre-clinical testing and yet to advance into human clinical trials. Meanwhile, systematic profiling of ADAR1-p150 expression in vital organs will be crucial to anticipate and mitigate systemic inflammation or other toxicities. Careful evaluation of context-specific mechanisms and monitoring normal tissue function will be essential for the development of safe and effective approaches to target ADAR1's Zα as an anti-cancer strategy. Continued integration of structural, biophysical and translational studies will be essential to define actionable biomarkers, sharpen mechanistic understanding, and guide the next generation of ADAR1-Zα-focused therapeutic strategies.

【Introduction · s0001-p3】Beyond subcellular localization, ADAR1-p150 is further distinguished from p110 by the presence of an additional N-terminal Zα domain that binds left-handed Z-DNA and Z-RNA (collectively referred to as Z-nucleic acids, ZNAs). 22 Our earlier work has demonstrated that the Zα domain of the ADAR1-p150 is required for its localization to the cytoplasmic stress granules. 23 Notably, this Zα domain is found in only one other protein among mammals, the Z-DNA-binding protein 1 (ZBP1). Defects in the ADAR1 Zα–ZNA axis unleash ZBP1-driven inflammatory signaling and/or regulated cell death programs. 24‐26 These three studies published in Nature demonstrated that ZBP1 acts as a key effector of immunopathology when ADAR1 Zα function is impaired, thereby establishing ZNAs sensing as biologically consequential and partially independent of canonical necroptosis pathways. 24 , 26 Concurrent structural, biochemical and mutagenesis studies have further refined ADAR1 domain architecture and enzymology, informing drug discovery efforts and suggesting that Zα-dependent functions extend beyond RNA editing per se. 27 , 28

【Figure 1. · f0001】Figure 1. Structural basis and cellular context of Z-nucleic acid (ZNA) recognition by ADAR1. (A) Comparative geometry of canonical right-handed helices (B-DNA and A-RNA) versus the non-canonical, left-handed Z-conformation. (B) Molecular architecture of the ADAR1's Zα domain (PDB ID: 1QBJ, https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb1QBJ/pdb). Key conserved residues (N173, Y177, P193, and W195) critical for conformational recognition, structural integrity, and potential pharmacological intervention are highlighted. (C) Spatial regulation of ADAR1 isoforms and the landscape of Z-RNA sensing. The constitutive p110 isoform is expressed predominantly in the nucleus, whereas the interferon (IFN)-inducible p150 isoform could shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm, but mainly localizes to the cytoplasm. Here, the Zα domain senses Z-RNA generated from inverted Alu repeats, integrating structural recognition with downstream RNA processing and the suppression of innate immune signaling pathways. Declaration: Figure concepts and illustrative icons namely B-DNA, A-RNA, Z-DNA/Z-RNA and Inverted Alu repeats were generated using Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google), with final vector assembly, editing, and accuracy verification performed manually in Microsoft PowerPoint.
